title: What information does a stack trace carry, how do you log an exception correctly (log.error("msg", ex): NOT ex.getMessage()), and how do you read a "Caused by:" chain?
shortTitle: How do you read and log stack traces correctly?
keyPoints: A stack trace shows the call chain from where the exception was thrown back to the entry point with class, method, file, and line number
Correct logging: log.error("msg {}", context, exception) where the exception is the LAST argument for SLF4J to print the full trace
Wrong: log.error(exception.getMessage()) loses the stack trace, line numbers, and cause chain completely
Wrong: exception.printStackTrace() writes to stderr, has no timestamp, is not thread-safe, and is lost in production
Read Caused by chains bottom-up: the LAST Caused by is the root cause that tells you what actually went wrong
Use getRootCause() utility to programmatically traverse to the deepest cause in the chain

s1_definition.oneliner: A stack trace shows the complete call chain with class, method, file, and line number for each frame, and must be logged correctly using log.error("msg", exception) with the throwable as the last argument.
s1_definition.profdef:
- A **stack trace** shows every method on the call stack when the exception was thrown: exception class, message, and each frame with class name, method name, file name, and line number.
- **Correct logging**: `log.error("Settlement failed for {}", tradeId, exception)` where the exception is the last argument. SLF4J detects the last argument is a Throwable and prints the full stack trace.
- **Wrong**: `log.error(exception.getMessage())` loses the stack trace and cause chain. `exception.printStackTrace()` writes to stderr (not log files), has no timestamp, and is not thread-safe.
- **Caused by chain**: read bottom-up. The last "Caused by:" is the root cause. Each level adds context from the service layer down to the infrastructure.
s1_definition.analogy: A stack trace is the incident report at National Bank of India. It says: "The error happened in TradeService.settle() at line 42, called by TradeController.execute() at line 18, called by DispatcherServlet." Correct logging hands the FULL report to the logging system. Wrong logging hands only the first sentence ("trade failed"), and investigators cannot find WHERE it happened.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Stack Trace Structure:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ RuntimeException: Settlement failed TRD-001 │ ← Business context
  │   at TradeService.settle(line 42)           │ ← Your code
  │   at TradeController.execute(line 18)       │ ← Framework
  │ Caused by: SQLException: Connection refused │ ← Technical layer
  │   at HikariPool.getConnection(line 128)     │
  │ Caused by: ConnectException: refused        │ ← ROOT CAUSE
  │   at Socket.connect(line 591)               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Read BOTTOM-UP for root cause.

  Correct:  log.error("msg {}", ctx, exception)
  Wrong:    log.error(exception.getMessage())
  Wrong:    exception.printStackTrace()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A stack trace carries the complete call chain from where the exception was thrown back to the entry point, with class, method, file, and line number for each frame. The "Caused by:" sections show exception chaining, and the root cause is always the last "Caused by:" at the bottom.

The correct way to log an exception is `log.error("Settlement failed for {}", tradeId, exception)` with the exception as the last argument. SLF4J detects it is a Throwable and prints the full stack trace including all "Caused by:" levels. Never use `log.error(exception.getMessage())` which loses the trace, line numbers, and cause chain. Never use `exception.printStackTrace()` in production because it writes to stderr, has no timestamp, and is not in your log files.

At National Bank of India, Rajesh always passes the exception object as the last argument to the logger. When the ops team investigates a settlement failure, they read the trace bottom-up: SettlementException (business context) caused by DataAccessException (technical layer) caused by ConnectException (root cause: database server down). Fix the infrastructure, not the code.

Remember one sentence: always log the exception object as the last argument so the full stack trace and cause chain are preserved.
